title: Versioning, Experiments & Rollout
summary: An agent's behavior is defined by more than code: its prompts, the model it calls, and its tool definitions all shape outputs, and changing any one can shift behavior invisibly. Treating these as a single versioned release — pinned together, tagged, and reproducible — lets you roll out changes safely. You gate promotions on eval results, ship gradually with canary and A/B rollouts, watch metrics, and roll back instantly to a known-good version when a release regresses.

subtopics.title: Version prompts, model, and tools as one unit
subtopics.explanation: An agent's behavior emerges from the interaction of its system prompt, the specific model version it calls, and the exact tool schemas it exposes — tweak any one and outputs can change in ways code review won't catch. Bundling all three into a single versioned artifact means a 'release' is a fully specified, comparable thing rather than a moving target. Versioning them together is the prerequisite for every safe-rollout technique that follows.
subtopics.example:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgentRelease:
    version: str                 # e.g. 'v2025.07.09-a'
    system_prompt: str           # the exact prompt text
    model: str                   # pinned model version, not 'latest'
    tool_schemas: tuple          # the exact tool definitions

release = AgentRelease(
    version="v2025.07.09-a",
    system_prompt="You are a support agent...",
    model="claude-x-2025-06",   # pin the snapshot, never a floating alias
    tool_schemas=("get_order", "issue_refund"),
)
# the whole triple is one comparable, shippable unit

subtopics.title: Make releases reproducible and pinned
subtopics.explanation: If a release points at a floating alias like 'model-latest' or reads a prompt from a mutable file, the same version can behave differently next week and you can't reproduce a past run. Pinning every input — model snapshot, prompt hash, tool schema hash, decoding params — makes a release a deterministic recipe you can rebuild and audit. Reproducibility is what lets you trust that an eval result or an incident is tied to a specific, recoverable configuration.
subtopics.example:
import hashlib, json

def release_fingerprint(release) -> str:
    payload = {
        "model": release.model,
        "prompt_sha": hashlib.sha256(release.system_prompt.encode()).hexdigest(),
        "tools": sorted(release.tool_schemas),
        "temperature": 0,
    }
    # a stable fingerprint identifies exactly what ran
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

print("release id:", release_fingerprint(release))

subtopics.title: Gate promotion on evals
subtopics.explanation: Because you can't eyeball whether a prompt tweak helped or hurt, a candidate release must clear an automated eval suite — accuracy, tool-call correctness, safety, cost, latency — before it's allowed to serve real traffic. The eval acts as a quality gate: pass and you may promote, regress and the pipeline blocks the release. Eval-gating turns 'it seemed better in a demo' into an objective, repeatable promotion decision.

subtopics.title: Roll out gradually with canary and A/B
subtopics.explanation: Even an eval-passing release can surprise you on live traffic, so you route a small slice (a canary, say 5%) to the new version first and compare its live metrics against the current one before widening. An A/B split does the same for a controlled comparison, measuring the new version against the incumbent on real users. Gradual rollout limits the blast radius of a bad release to a fraction of traffic instead of everyone at once.
subtopics.example:
import random

def route(user_id: str, canary_pct: float, stable, canary):
    # deterministic bucketing so a user stays on one version
    bucket = (hash(user_id) % 100) / 100.0
    return canary if bucket < canary_pct else stable

# 5% canary: most users hit stable, a small slice tests the new release
chosen = route("user-42", canary_pct=0.05, stable="v1", canary="v2")
print("serving version:", chosen)

subtopics.title: Roll back instantly to a known-good version
subtopics.explanation: When canary metrics regress — accuracy drops, cost spikes, unsafe outputs rise — you need to revert in seconds, not redeploy for minutes. Because releases are pinned, immutable artifacts, rollback is just pointing the traffic router back at the previous version's fingerprint. Fast, boring rollback is the safety net that makes aggressive iteration acceptable, because any mistake is quickly and completely reversible.

foundations.overview: A production agent's behavior is not fully captured by its source code. Its outputs are governed jointly by the system prompt, the exact model version it calls, and the tool schemas it exposes — so a prompt tweak or a silent model update can shift behavior in ways ordinary code review never sees. The discipline is to treat those three as one versioned, pinned, reproducible release; gate any candidate release behind an automated eval suite so only measured improvements are allowed to promote; roll out gradually with a canary and/or A/B split so a bad release affects a small slice of traffic rather than everyone; and keep rollback to a previous immutable release instant. Together these turn agent changes from risky, hard-to-attribute edits into safe, measurable, reversible releases.
foundations.formalDefinition: An agent release is an immutable, fingerprinted bundle of {system prompt, pinned model snapshot, tool schemas, decoding params}. Rollout is the controlled promotion of a release — gated by passing an eval suite, exposed to progressively larger traffic slices via canary/A-B routing, monitored against the incumbent, and reversible by repointing traffic to a prior release.
foundations.whyItMatters: Small, invisible changes to prompts or models can cause large behavioral shifts, and without versioning you can neither attribute a regression nor reproduce a good result. Eval-gated, gradual, reversible rollout is what lets teams iterate quickly on agents without periodically shipping a silent quality or safety regression to all users.
foundations.mentalModel: Treat an agent release like a software release with a lockfile. The prompt, model snapshot, and tool schemas are the pinned dependencies; the eval suite is CI that must go green before deploy; the canary is shipping to 5% of servers first; and rollback is flipping the load balancer back to the previous build. Nothing floats, everything is tagged, and every change is measured before it goes wide.
commonUseCases: Shipping a prompt or model change without a silent regression
A/B testing two prompts or models on live traffic
Canarying a new tool definition to a small slice first
Reproducing and auditing exactly what configuration produced a past output

commonMisconceptions.myth: Only the code needs versioning; prompts and models are just config.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Prompts, the model snapshot, and tool schemas jointly determine behavior. If they aren't versioned together, a 'no-code' change can silently alter outputs and you can't reproduce or attribute it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If it passed evals, it's safe to roll out to everyone at once.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Evals catch a lot but never everything live traffic surfaces. You still canary/A-B a small slice first and watch real metrics before going wide.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Pinning to 'model-latest' keeps you up to date safely.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A floating alias means the provider can change your agent's behavior with no release on your side — unreproducible and unattributable. Pin a specific model snapshot and upgrade as a deliberate, eval-gated release.

checkpoints.prompt: Why version the prompt, model, and tool schemas together as one release?
options: To reduce the number of files in the repo
Because all three jointly determine the agent's behavior, so a change to any one can silently shift outputs unless it's captured in a comparable, reproducible unit
To make the model run faster
checkpoints.explanation: Behavior emerges from the interaction of prompt, model version, and tool schemas. If they aren't bundled and pinned together, a 'config-only' change can alter outputs with nothing in code review to catch it, and you can't reproduce or attribute the result.

checkpoints.prompt: A candidate release passes the full eval suite. What's the correct next step?
options: Ship it to 100% of traffic immediately
Route a small canary slice and compare live metrics before widening
Delete the previous version to save space
Skip monitoring since evals already passed
checkpoints.explanation: Passing evals is necessary but not sufficient — live traffic surfaces things offline evals miss. You canary a small slice (or A/B split), watch real metrics against the incumbent, and only then widen the rollout.

checkpoints.prompt: What makes instant rollback possible when a canary regresses?
options: The new version is automatically deleted
Releases are immutable, fingerprinted artifacts, so rollback is just repointing the traffic router at the previous known-good release — no redeploy
The provider reverts the model for you
You retrain the model on the fly
checkpoints.explanation: Because each release is a pinned, immutable artifact identified by a fingerprint, reverting is a routing change — flip traffic back to the prior version in seconds. Fast, reversible rollback is the safety net that makes aggressive iteration acceptable.

keyTakeaways: An agent's behavior is set by prompt + model snapshot + tool schemas together, so version and pin all three as one immutable release.
Never point at a floating 'latest' alias — pin a specific model snapshot so releases are reproducible and attributable.
Gate every candidate release behind an automated eval suite (accuracy, tool correctness, safety, cost, latency) before it can serve traffic.
Roll out gradually with a canary and/or A/B split, bucketing users deterministically and comparing live metrics before widening.
Keep rollback instant: repoint traffic to the previous known-good release in seconds — fast reversibility is what makes fast iteration safe.
